citation: Li S-L, Ferrari MJ, Bjornstad ON, Runge MC, Fonnesbeck CJ, Tildesley MJ, Pannell D, Shea K (2019) Concurrent assessment of epidemiological and operational uncertainties for optimal outbreak control: Ebola as a case study. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 286:20190774
licence: CC BY 4.0 (article and electronic supplementary material)
retrieved: 2026-11-25, article PDF and the four supplementary files (rspb20190774supp1.xlsx to supp4.txt) supplied by the user; Table S3 converted cell by cell from rspb20190774supp3.xlsx by a script, which checked that there are 999 rows (37 models x 27 combinations), that no value has more than three decimals, and that the workbook's 'Minimum' column equals the least of the three caseloads in every row and budget; Table 2 read from a text extraction of the PDF
decision: Which of three interventions to prioritise in an Ebola outbreak: reducing community transmission, reducing funeral transmission or improving hospitalisation
unit: cases in a simulated population of 10,000 (mean of 1000 stochastic simulations of each published model); lower is better, so payoffs are minus the caseload
baseline_note: The paper simulated a no-intervention baseline but prints its caseloads only as curves (Fig. 4), so there is no no-intervention column. The reference here is reducing community transmission, the intervention that is best on average under present knowledge at every budget, which is also what the paper measures every improvement against.
weights: equal weight on the 37 models and on the 27 cost function combinations (Methods)

table_s3.provenance: Electronic supplementary material, Table S3 (rspb20190774supp3.xlsx): caseload under each intervention for each of 37 Ebola models and 27 cost function combinations at three budget levels

ours.note: Counts from Table S3 at the low budget of the models in which the intervention has the lowest caseload when it has cost function 1 or 3 and both others have cost function 2. The text quotes 36 of 37 (funeral) and 31 of 37 (hospitalisation) 'in both cases'. No single cost function combination of Table S3, at any budget, gives 36 for funeral or 31 for hospitalisation, so these two counts are not reproduced and the reason is not known; the article's Table 1, from which they were presumably counted, is a picture and was not transcribed. The count for community transmission (37 of 37) is reproduced.

resolution: Every cell of Table 2 is reproduced from Table S3 to the precision printed, and so are the counts 16 of 27 and 22 of 37 of the text; two other counts of the text are not (see 'ours'). The Results text says that resolving operational uncertainty improves the outcome 'by 11.3% and 13.1% under intermediate and low budget levels, respectively'; Table 2 and our calculation give 11.3% at the low budget and 13.1% at the intermediate one, and the next sentence of the text itself uses 11.3% for the low budget, so the two figures are transposed in that sentence.

not_replicated.items: The simulations behind Table S3 (37 published models, 1000 stochastic runs each, in the authors' R script), Table S1, the curves of Figs. 3 and 4, and the scaling to the 2014 outbreak ('3753 fewer cases')
not_replicated.reason: The case study starts from the published caseloads, as the paper's own value-of-information analysis does; the authors' script is not translated or run.
